steps.say: Here is the task. A photograph dissolves into its depth map: red is near, blue is far, the sky is black.

right.say: Marigold showed that a fine-tuned image generator also makes a strong depth estimator. But after fine-tuning, it no longer generates images.

scenes.title: Depth, written as an image
scenes.sub: So the existing autoencoder can read it unchanged
scenes.say: Chapter two. Depth, written as an image.

scenes.text: Encode depth as an image with the same autoencoder, put it in the same token sequence, and let one transformer denoise picture and depth together.
scenes.say: Here's the idea. Encode depth as an image, with the same autoencoder. Put it in the same token sequence. And let one transformer denoise both.

steps.say: Start with the distance along each pixel's ray.
Take its log.
Map this image's own percentile range onto minus one to zero point nine five.
The sky goes to plus one, with a margin before it.

steps.term: Affine-invariant: right up to a scale and shift
steps.say: Copy it into three channels and encode it like any photo. Because the range is set per image, the depth is relative: right up to a scale and shift in log space.
The report's whole architecture. A prompt, an image and a depth map, through the backbone's own encoders.
Their tokens form one sequence, and one transformer denoises it.
Out come a picture and its depth. No depth head, no second network.
Take a five hundred and twelve pixel square picture.
The autoencoder makes a thirty-two by thirty-two grid, each cell a hundred and twenty-eight channels.
Each cell is one token: one thousand and twenty-four image tokens.
The depth map adds another thousand and twenty-four, right after them in the same sequence.

params.depth: its depth: red near, blue far
params.strip: text, then image tokens, then depth tokens
legend: Cut both into patches, one token per patch
Text, then all image tokens, then all depth tokens
Same row and column for each pair
A time axis the backbone already had
Each grid has its own noise level

steps.say: Cut the picture and its depth map into patches. Each patch becomes one token.
They join one sequence: the text, then every image token, then every depth token.

steps.term: Rotary position: where a token sits
steps.say: How does the model tell them apart? First, a depth token has the same row and column as its image patch, so attention knows they describe the same point.
Second, a time coordinate the backbone already used to keep reference images apart: zero for image, one for depth.

Third, a learned modality embedding of four rows says which role each token plays. It is the only new tensor: twenty-four thousand five hundred and seventy-six parameters, on a thirty-two billion parameter model.
And each grid gets its own noise level, so one can be generated while the other is given clean.

scenes.title: Four tasks, same weights
scenes.say: With that sequence, the four tasks differ only in what starts as noise.

items.say: Both noisy: a picture with its depth.
Photo given clean: only depth is denoised.
Depth given clean: paint a picture onto it.
Depth left as noise: a plain image generator.

steps.say: Give depth clean, and the picture is painted onto it. One Colosseum depth map, a sunken ruin under the sea.
Then a neon city, a jungle ruin, a castle of sand. Four prompts, one geometry.

scenes.title: How a benchmark depth is sampled

steps.say: For the benchmarks, image to depth runs four steps from noise, with the photo given clean.
From ten different seeds. That is forty transformer passes per picture.
Each seed is aligned to the first with a scale and shift in log space.
Then a per-pixel median. About fifteen seconds a picture for the big model, where the leading specialist takes zero point four one.

steps.term: AbsRel: mean relative error, lower is better
steps.say: The headline, on Marigold's five benchmarks: two point nine two against three point one two for the leading specialist. Lower is better.
But read panel c. Iris-Z only passes the specialist at forty passes. At one seed, the SDK's default, it is slightly behind.
